extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy (Aristotle's Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative criteria concerning self-love, friendship, the happy life, and pleasure as presented in Books IX–X of the Nicomachean Ethics. Useful for philosophical analysis, teaching, or close reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-loving (vulgar/disparaging sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who, with respect to wealth, honours, and bodily pleasures, give themselves the larger share; covetous, gratify lusts and the irrational part of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the common, reproachable sense of 'self-loving' — people who pursue apparent advantage (money, honours, bodily pleasures) are rightly blamed. Originates from the mass of mankind; exemplified by covetousness and passion-driven behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-loving (true/noble sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who give themselves the most noble and best things, gratify the highest principle (intellect/reason) of their nature, and obey it in everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This self-love is praiseworthy: the good man is ‘self-loving’ in this sense because he secures what is noblest for himself (virtue, honour), even sacrificing money or life for friends or country. Distinguish from vulgar self-love by the object and guiding principle (reason vs passion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship criterion: wishing good for the other's sake
rubrics_metrics.description: A friend is one who wishes good to another for that person's sake (even when no one knows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This desire for the other's good (not for one's own advantage) is the central mark of true friendship; many proverbs and ordinary paradoxes (one soul, goods of friends are common) reflect that friendship arises from self-regard extended to another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three kinds of friendship (useful, pleasurable, virtuous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships are classified as those based on utility, on pleasure, or on goodness/virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful friends are sought in adversity; pleasure-friends relate to enjoyment; virtuous friendships (friends for the other's sake) are highest and most stable. Evaluate a friendship by its motive/object rather than merely outward signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good man's relation to friends (second self / communion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The good man treats his friend as a second Self: shares words, thoughts, actions, and takes pleasure in the friend's good and actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship is deepened by living and acting together; the friend’s existence becomes choiceworthy similarly to one’s own. Intimacy (communion) is a key feature and aim of virtuous friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good conduct as self-love (preference for noble actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The good person prefers great, noble deeds (even brief) to tame, long-lived ease; will forego money and honours for the good and for friends/country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts such as dying for friends/country, giving up resources so friends receive more (but oneself gains honour), and preferring one great noble action to many trifling ones exemplify self-loving in the noble sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship improves virtue (mutual correction/practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Living with and sharing life with good people improves one's virtue through repeated acts and mutual correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship with the good transmits good impressions and habits; friendship is educational and formative (quoting poet: 'Thou from the good, good things shalt surely learn').

rubrics_metrics.name: Happy person needs friends (despite independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the Happy (self-sufficient) person requires friends for benefactions, objects for his benefactions, companionship for pleasurable and continuous activity, and contemplation of good actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against the notion that complete independence obviates friendship: functioning (living/working) is active, requires objects and persons; friends supply contexts for virtuous activity and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of friends: intimacy-limited
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a limited (non-definite) maximum number of friends with whom one can maintain genuine intimacy; one cannot be intimate with many at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having more friends than one can properly requite or be intimate with makes them officious or shallow; famous friendships are typically between two. Balance sufficiency for intimacy over sheer numerosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality over quantity in friendships
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a few truly virtuous/intimate friends rather than many superficial ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is difficult to be a friend to many for the sake of their virtue; contentment lies in finding a few such friends. Over-complaisance (meeting everybody as intimate) indicates lack of true friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical guidance on calling friends in good vs bad fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Call friends in readily on occasions of good fortune (to share/forward) but be more reluctant to involve them in your misfortunes; only call them when their inconvenience is small and the benefit to you great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nobility calls for sharing good fortune; avoid needlessly making friends share in your ills. The maxim 'I am unfortunate, let that suffice' illustrates restrained solicitation of sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to aid friends in misfortune (go unasked)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fitting to go to one's friends in their misfortunes unasked and with alacrity; kindness in need is a friend’s office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive assistance to friends in trouble is more creditable and pleasant to both; in their good fortune, go to them if you can forward it, but be cautious in sharing their gains or seeming eager to receive advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social sensitivity when declining help
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid presenting the appearance of sullenness when declining sympathy or help from friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor social guidance: be cautious of appearing aloof or sullen, as this can damage friendship even when one is justified in declining assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as limited by emotional capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong emotions (love, deep friendship) must be limited in number; one cannot deeply love or be intimate with many objects simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical reason: difficulty sympathising with simultaneous joys and sorrows of many friends; emotional intensity requires limitation (parallel to being in love which typically implies one object).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as candidate for the chief good (Eudoxus' test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eudoxus argues Pleasure is the Chief Good because all things (rational and irrational) aim at it; it is chosen for its own sake and increases the choiceworthiness of other goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle presents and critiques Eudoxus' arguments: unanimity of aim is not decisive, 'chosen for its own sake' does not prove supreme status, and combination with other goods complicates the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique: Pleasure is not necessarily the Chief Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure's being widely aimed at does not establish it as the highest good; pleasures differ in kind and quality, and many goods are chosen irrespective of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle challenges arguments that Pain’s avoidance proves Pleasure’s goodness, that Pleasure’s additivity proves primacy, and that being an act/ movement disqualifies or qualifies it. He notes examples of pleasures (mathematical, memories) not linked to bodily supply or prior lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of pleasures by source and moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures differ in kind according to their object: pleasures from honourable objects differ from those from disgraceful ones; the pleasure of being just requires being just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some pleasures are 'mixed' or 'unmixed'; deplorable pleasures (felt by the ill-disposed) are not 'really' pleasant in the moral sense (analogy to sick people perceiving tastes/colors incorrectly). Evaluate pleasures by their source and alignment with virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is not merely bodily supply after lack
rubrics_metrics.description: The account that Pain is lack and Pleasure a supply (bodily restoration) is inadequate: many pleasures (mathematical, smells, memories, hopes) are not supplies after a prior lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This undermines reductive physiological accounts of pleasure; evaluate pleasures beyond bodily hunger/thirst analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure increases choiceworthiness of virtuous acts but is not their sole value
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding pleasure to virtuous actions makes them more choiceworthy, but that does not prove pleasure is the Chief Good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle accepts that pleasure enhances goods but insists some activities remain choiceworthy even without pleasure (seeing, knowing, possessing excellences). Thus pleasure is contributory, not necessarily primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friend vs flatterer diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish friend (aims at the other's good) from flatterer (aims at producing pleasure); this distinction exposes differences in the moral quality of pleasures and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the motives and objects of intercourse to tell whether someone is a true friend or a flatterer; flattering that aims only at pleasure is reproached, whereas friendship aiming at good is praised.
